exam.notes: Written or oral, announced in lecture 4.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a 1:n and an n:m relationship in the ER model and how each turns into tables.
questions.answer:
- 1:n: each entity on the n side is related to at most one on the 1 side; becomes a foreign key on the n side.
- n:m: both sides many; needs its own table with both keys (and the relationship's attributes).

questions.prompt: Why does a weak entity need an identifying relationship?
questions.answer:
- It has no key of its own (only a partial key).
- Its key is formed together with the key of the owner entity via the identifying relationship.
- Example: a room is identified by building + room number.

topics.title: Relational algebra
topics.notes: Selection, projection, join, division; translation to SQL.

questions.prompt: Explain what a natural join does, and what happens if the two relations have no attribute in common.
questions.answer:
- Combines tuples that agree on all attributes with the same name; common attributes appear once.
- With no common attribute it becomes the Cartesian product.

questions.prompt: Write a relational algebra expression for the names of all students in semester 3, given Student(id, name, semester).
questions.answer:
- π_name(σ_semester=3(Student)).
- Selection first filters the rows, projection then keeps the name column; duplicates disappear in set semantics.

topics.title: SQL: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY
topics.notes: Evaluation order, HAVING vs. WHERE, NULL semantics.

questions.prompt: Why can you not use an aggregate like COUNT(*) in WHERE, and where does such a condition go instead?
questions.answer:
- WHERE filters single rows before grouping; aggregates only exist per group.
- Conditions on aggregates go into HAVING, which filters groups after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: What if you replace an INNER JOIN by a LEFT JOIN: which extra rows can appear in the result?
questions.answer:
- All rows of the left table are kept.
- Rows without a match get NULL in the columns of the right table.
- Typical use: also list customers without orders.

questions.prompt: Explain what 3NF requires and give an example of a violation.
questions.answer:
- 2NF plus: no non-key attribute depends transitively on a key (no FD between non-key attributes).
- Example: Student(id, zip, city) with zip → city; city depends on id only via zip.
- Fix: split into Student(id, zip) and Zip(zip, city).

questions.prompt: Why is BCNF stricter than 3NF, and what can you lose when you decompose into BCNF?
questions.answer:
- BCNF: the left side of every non-trivial FD is a superkey; 3NF also allows FDs whose right side is a key attribute (prime).
- A BCNF decomposition is always lossless but not always dependency-preserving.
